name: Dana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six hundred acres of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, and a flock of fifty ewes that graze the stubbles, mostly because my husband likes them. In November the drilling's done, so my day is grain marketing, which means deciding when to sell what's in the store. I'm at the kitchen table by seven with coffee and three screens, checking prices in four markets, then out to the grain store to check temperatures, because a hot spot in the heap can ruin a hundred tonnes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love selling well. Last March I sold two hundred tonnes of wheat on the one good day of the month and I danced round the kitchen. What wears me out is harvest, six weeks of sixteen-hour days, and the weather, which no screen in the world can fix.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's on the farm with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mark, my husband, retired from the police and now does the sheep and the paperwork. One full-time worker, Ollie, who's thirty-five and drives the combine better than anyone. Two students at harvest. Our son Ben is a lawyer, and our daughter Jo is an architect.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day. It summarises the market reports, it helps me plan which fields get how much fertiliser, and it drafts my letters. I argue with it like a colleague. It's wrong about grain prices about as often as my old adviser was, but it costs less and answers at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, use it or don't, your choice. I'd tell the young farmers' group they're mad not to try it, but I wouldn't preach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's how things already are. If it stays a handy tool, I keep my edge on the marketing side. Fine by me. I'd rather have a small edge that lasts than a big change nobody understands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Upgrade the yield mapping on the combine, around eight thousand. Try the AI on the sheep records for Mark. Keep Ollie on and give him the usual rise. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit pleased with myself for getting in early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the edge, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Timing. Most farmers round here sell when the merchant rings them. I sell when the numbers say so. Over five years that's been worth about twelve pounds a tonne to me, which on our tonnage is real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mark use it on the sheep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd pretend not to and then use it at night. He did the same with the smartphone. I caught him asking it how to treat foot rot in ewes and he said he was just checking it was wrong.

S0.say: It's a good tool, so use it or don't, your choice. I'd tell the young farmers' group they're mad not to try it, but I wouldn't preach.
S0.think: It's how things already are for me, and I keep my edge on grain marketing. I'd rather have a small edge that lasts than a big change nobody understands.
S0.do: Upgrades yield mapping on the combine for around eight thousand and tries AI on her husband's sheep records. Keeps her worker Ollie on with the usual rise and makes no dramatic changes.
S0.feel: Calm, and a bit pleased with herself for getting in early.
S0.quote: I caught him asking it how to treat foot rot in ewes and he said he was just checking it was wrong.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is confident and businesslike, and she counts her advantage in pounds per tonne. She treats AI like a colleague she argues with. There's warm humour in how she describes her husband's secret use of the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is manageable. Hiring fewer beginners is a problem though, and I'd say business and government both need to pay their share for apprenticeships. Not one or the other, both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow suits me. I've got a head start, and the others won't catch up fast. But I'd worry about the farm students we take on at harvest. If firms stop hiring young people, they'll lean on summer jobs like ours more, and we can only take two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take on a third harvest student, around four thousand for the summer. Buy the next level of crop-mapping drone, which I'd have bought anyway, about eleven thousand. Spend time showing Ollie the planning side, so he's learning more than driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly uneasy, about young people mostly. For the farm, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach Ollie the planning side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the driving part will go first, eventually. Tractors already steer themselves by satellite. The bit that won't go so quickly is knowing that field nine always floods in the bottom corner. Ollie knows that, and he should be paid for knowing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ollie want to learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. He likes the cab and his music. I'd have to sell it to him as a pay rise, which it would be. He's sensible, he'll come round when he sees the money.

S1.say: Slow change is manageable. Hiring fewer beginners is a problem, and business and government both need to pay their share for apprenticeships, not one or the other.
S1.think: Slow suits me because I've got a head start the others won't close quickly. I'd worry about the harvest students, since we can only take two and more would be looking.
S1.do: Takes on a third harvest student for about four thousand and buys a better crop-mapping drone for about eleven thousand. Starts teaching her worker Ollie the planning side, framed as a pay rise.
S1.feel: Mildly uneasy about young people, and fine about the farm.
S1.quote: The bit that won't go so quickly is knowing that field nine always floods in the bottom corner.
S1.fieldNote: She is already thinking about which parts of her worker's job will go first and moving him early. Her centre politics come out as shared responsibility between business and government. She is matter-of-fact about Ollie, but clearly values him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was coming and anyone who's surprised hasn't been paying attention. Help people retrain, yes, and fast. But politicians shouting at each other won't stop it, so they should spend the energy on the help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be one of the people buying those assistants. I'd probably drop the grain marketing adviser, which saves me four thousand a year. He's a nice man called Graham, and I've used him for fifteen years. I'd feel bad about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up an assistant to handle the farm office, the contracts, the payment claims. Tell Graham face to face that I'm stopping, not by email, and give him a good word to others. Look at offering my marketing know-how to two or three neighbours for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited about the tools. Guilty about Graham. A bit worried for Ben and Jo, though I think they're far enough up the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that conversation with Graham go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, I expect. He'd say he saw it coming. He'd probably ask if I wanted to keep him on for the big decisions only. I might, at half the fee. I'd try to find a way that wasn't just cutting him off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ben and Jo are far enough up the ladder. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I said that to make myself feel better. Ben's a lawyer, and a lot of what young lawyers do is read documents, which these things do well. He's thirty-three, he's not that senior. I should ring him.

S2.say: It was coming, and anyone surprised hasn't been paying attention. Help people retrain fast, and politicians should spend their energy on help instead of shouting.
S2.think: I'd be one of the people buying those assistants, and I'd probably drop my grain adviser Graham to save four thousand a year. I've used him fifteen years and I'd feel bad.
S2.do: Sets up an assistant for the farm office, contracts and payment claims. Tells Graham in person she's stopping, perhaps keeping him at half fee for big decisions, and offers her own marketing know-how to neighbours for a fee.
S2.feel: Excited about the tools, guilty about her adviser, and more worried for her lawyer son than she first admitted.
S2.quote: No. I said that to make myself feel better. Ben's a lawyer, and a lot of what young lawyers do is read documents, which these things do well.
S2.fieldNote: She caught her own reassurance about her children and dropped it when pushed. Her decision about Graham is clear-headed but she cares how it's done. She sees new business in selling her own skill to neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a deal both sides can live with. Tax the gains enough to look after the people who lost out, but not so much that nobody invests. It's not complicated, it's just politics making it complicated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this one is about Ben and Jo, not me. A lawyer and an architect are exactly the skilled thinking jobs on that card. They've both got mortgages, and Jo's just had a baby. The farm would be fine, which makes it worse somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring them both that week and talk money, properly. Tell them we can cover their mortgages for six months each if it comes to it, which we can, I've worked it out. Keep the farm steady. Maybe sell some shares at the top of the boom, because booms that fast end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's strange to be the farmer with the safe job while my children with their degrees are the ones at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo, with the new baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she's not to panic, that she can come home with the baby for as long as she likes. And that architects who can use these tools will be fine longer than ones who can't. Then I'd probably send her some links, and she'd tell me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been very calm in every picture so far. Is this the first one that gets to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My own work I can plan for. Your children, you can't plan their lives for them, even if you've got a spreadsheet for everything else.

S3.say: We need a deal both sides can live with. Tax the gains enough to look after those who lost out, but not so much that nobody invests.
S3.think: This one is about Ben and Jo, not me. A lawyer and an architect are exactly the jobs on that card, they have mortgages, and Jo's just had a baby.
S3.do: Rings both children that week to talk money and offers to cover each mortgage for six months, which she has worked out the farm can afford. Keeps the farm steady and sells some shares at the top of the boom.
S3.feel: Anxious, and unsettled to be the farmer with the safe job while her degree-holding children are at risk.
S3.quote: Your children, you can't plan their lives for them, even if you've got a spreadsheet for everything else.
S3.fieldNote: This is where her calm breaks, and only because of her children. She responds the way she always does, with numbers, then admits numbers don't cover it. She already has the mortgage figure worked out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms aren't the end of the world if we manage it. Help for workers, help for smaller farms, and honest talk about what's coming. I'd be the person at the meeting saying don't panic, plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be first in the queue for a self-driving tractor and a robot that walks the crops pulling weeds. I've wanted one for years. The hard part is Ollie. If a robot drives the tractor, I've got a man with fifteen years of skill and nothing to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lease one robot tractor in the first year, roughly thirty thousand, and put Ollie in charge of running it. Start a small contracting business with Ollie running robots for neighbouring farms who can't afford their own. Put him on a share of the profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, more than scared. And worried for the village. If every farm needs one person instead of four, the school and the pub start closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ollie go for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if the money's right. I'd make it worth his while, a share of the contracting profit, not just wages. He's got a daughter starting school, he'd want security more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't panic, plan. What's the part you can't plan for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The village emptying. I can save my farm and probably Ollie's job. I can't keep the pub open by myself. That one's beyond a spreadsheet as well.

S4.say: Robots on farms aren't the end of the world if we manage it, with help for workers and smaller farms and honest talk. I'd be the one at the meeting saying don't panic, plan.
S4.think: I'd be first in the queue for a self-driving tractor and a weeding robot. The hard part is Ollie, who would have fifteen years of skill and nothing to drive.
S4.do: Leases one robot tractor for roughly thirty thousand in the first year and puts Ollie in charge of it. Starts a small contracting business with Ollie running robots for neighbours, giving him a share of the profit.
S4.feel: Excited more than scared, but worried about the village emptying as farms need fewer people.
S4.quote: If every farm needs one person instead of four, the school and the pub start closing.
S4.fieldNote: She turns the threat into a business with her worker as a partner, which is her adaptive instinct at its strongest. The anxiety that's left is about the village, not her farm. She uses the same 'beyond a spreadsheet' idea again, showing where her confidence runs out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast AI one, the one before the robots, because of Ben and Jo. The robots I can handle. What would help is a proper safety net for people mid-career, something that pays a decent share of your wage while you retrain, not a pittance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the villages. Everyone's talking about jobs one by one. Nobody adds up what happens when a whole valley needs a quarter of the people. That's the number I'd want someone to work out.

headlineQuote: Your children, you can't plan their lives for them, even if you've got a spreadsheet for everything else.
portrait: Dana Kowalski is fifty-eight and farms six hundred acres of grain and oilseed with her husband Mark and one worker, Ollie. She uses AI all day, sells grain by the numbers, and treats change as something to plan for. Her views are in the middle: shared responsibility, a fair deal, less shouting. She stays calm until the fast AI picture, when her lawyer son and architect daughter are the ones at risk and she admits her spreadsheets can't help. In the robot picture she'd be first in the queue and would start a contracting business with Ollie as a partner, though she worries about the village emptying.
biggestWorry: The fast AI picture, because her lawyer son and architect daughter would be at risk, which she can't plan away.
whatWouldHelp: A proper safety net for mid-career people that pays a decent share of their wage while they retrain.
